name: Person Shrugging
baseMeaning: A picture of a figure with both arms raised, palms turned up. Read in a message it lands as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter.
tldr: 🤷 Person Shrugging. In a chat it comes across as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter.

contextMeanings.meaning: The plain reading: a figure with both arms raised, palms turned up. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Answering a question you did not expect 🤷

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter.
contextMeanings.example: Declining to take blame for a group decision 🤷

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.

platformNotes.note: In Slack 🤷 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for answering a question you did not expect, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 🤷 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 🤷 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like declining to take blame for a group decision. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Person Shrugging 🤷 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like answering a question you did not expect is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

WhatsApp renders 🤷 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the person section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like declining to take blame for a group decision.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reaches for 🤷 to do the work of answering a question you did not expect, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter.

Millennials tend to send 🤷 deliberately, usually for something like declining to take blame for a group decision, and they read saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 🤷 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 🤷 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter subtext in it.

seoTitle: 🤷 Person Shrugging Emoji - What It Actually Means in Text
seoDescription: 🤷 Person Shrugging meaning: saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter. How the emoji is used at work, at home and in dating threads, and where it goes wrong.

longForm.overview:
The drawing of 🤷 is a figure with both arms raised, palms turned up. It arrived with Unicode 9.0 in the person section, and in a conversation it does the work of a line somebody left out on purpose.

The line it stands in for is saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one — a picture carries the same meaning as the sentence it replaces, and it arrives first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets mistaken for an apology when it usually refuses to take responsibility, since the palms-up gesture hands the problem back to the room. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🤨 Face With Raised Eyebrow: the raised eyebrow questions one specific claim, the shrug questions everything and moves on. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

The person shrugging also exists in five skin tones. They are separate pages with separate copy, because picking a tone is a decision in a way that picking the plain emoji is not: it says something about who the sender thinks the reader is.

In short — the person shrugging reads as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter, it is most often used for answering a question you did not expect or declining to take blame for a group decision, and the five tone pages under it each say something different about who is sending it. The rest of the page takes those three apart.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
Context, not the picture, decides how this lands. 🤷 in a work thread is declining to take blame for a group decision; 🤷 in a family thread is answering a question you did not expect; 🤷 in a thread with somebody you like is a way of saying something you would rather not type out.

The tone versions of the emoji make the same point from the other side. The gesture is identical in all five, and the swatch says something about the sender before a word is read.

The shortest messages are the risky ones. A lone 🤷 is the whole reply, and it is carrying a meaning nobody wrote down — saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter is the intention, but what arrives is a drawing. Everything the sentence would have disambiguated is simply missing.

Put it this way. Answering a question you did not expect is the job the person shrugging does most: it saves a sentence and lands faster than one would have. Declining to take blame for a group decision is the job it does second: there the picture is not the point, it is the temperature of the message.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Think about what the emoji is replacing. If the sentence under it is doing the real work, 🤷 will get mistaken for an apology when it usually refuses to take responsibility, since the palms-up gesture hands the problem back to the room instead, and the thread ends up carrying a meaning nobody wrote.

And keep it away from first contact. There is nothing warm in the drawing, and a person shrugging gesture used to answer other people's messages tends to sound like it is settling a point.

Keep it out of the formal register. In a thread about somebody's work, or in a message to somebody you have not met, 🤷 reads as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter, and formality is exactly where that reading does the most damage.

Leave 🤨 Face With Raised Eyebrow for the other message. The raised eyebrow questions one specific claim, the shrug questions everything and moves on. And keep 🤷 out of threads where somebody is hurting: it reads as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter there, because there is nothing in the drawing that says you meant well.
longForm.howToReply:
The safe move in an unclear thread is to answer the text. 🤷 gets mistaken for an apology when it usually refuses to take responsibility, since the palms-up gesture hands the problem back to the room often enough that the sentence matters more than the picture.

And do not send 🤷 alone when the message underneath is supposed to be warm. A message like answering a question you did not expect carries the feeling; the picture on its own leaves the reader choosing between saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter and something sharper.

Start by reading what the 🤷 was doing. If it was a reaction, react: 🤷 back, and the thread is closed. If it was aimed at you, write. The difference matters, because the reply to a reaction can be a picture and the reply to a request cannot.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🤷 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under person shrugging show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 🤷 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🤷 is used for saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter. The drawing shows a figure with both arms raised, palms turned up, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🤷 and 🤨?
faqs.answer: The raised eyebrow questions one specific claim, the shrug questions everything and moves on. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 🤷 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter, but it gets mistaken for an apology when it usually refuses to take responsibility, since the palms-up gesture hands the problem back to the room. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 🤷 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

conversationExamples.interpretation: A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: answering a question you did not expect 🤷
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: declining to take blame for a group decision 🤷
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 🤷
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets mistaken for an apology when it usually refuses to take responsibility, since the palms-up gesture hands the problem back to the room more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.

conversationExamples.message: answering a question you did not expect 🤷
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is saying nobody knows, or that it does not matter, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
